title: Above the bathhouse
hookLine: Seneca lodges over a noisy bath and practices calm inside the racket (Letters 56)

lines: A ROOM ABOVE A BUSY GYM.
cards: A room right above a busy gym. Not a quiet yoga studio: a weight room with dropped barbells, a sauna, a snack bar, and a man who sings in the shower because he loves the echo.
That's roughly where Seneca is living when he writes the fifty-sixth letter, in a lodging right over a public bath. He decides to treat it as a test.
If a philosopher's calm is real, surely it can survive a few grunts and splashes.

teach.b: The weightlifters grunt and gasp as they swing their weights. The masseur slaps shoulders, and Seneca can tell from the sound whether it's a flat hand or a cupped one.
A ball player arrives and starts counting his points out loud, and that's the end of it.

Add a quarrel, a thief caught in the act, the man who loves his voice in the bath, people jumping into the pool with a huge splash, the hair-plucker's shrill cry, and the sellers of drinks, sausages and pastries, each with a special call.

I don't care about any of it, Seneca says, any more than about waves or a waterfall. Noise outside can't reach a mind that's settled. What disturbs us is the racket inside: worry, ambition, desire, all shouting at once.
A person can lie in a silent room and be in uproar. Then the twist. At the very end, Seneca admits the test is a bit of a show.
Why torture myself any longer? he asks. I'm going to move out.
Calm inside is the goal, and training in the noise is useful.
But there's no prize for staying in a racket you can leave.
Learn quiet inside, then, if you're able, choose a quieter room.

how: Some people practice sitting calmly in ordinary noise, letting sounds pass without reacting, while still choosing quieter places when they can.

o: a silent room far away from the city's noise
a Roman public bath with hot and cold pools
calm of mind, settled even in the middle of noise

games.q: the noisy bath — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca stays above the bath forever to prove his calm
at the end he asks why torture himself, and decides to move.
Seneca says the noise inside us is the real disturbance
a person can lie in a silent room and be in uproar.
Seneca could tell a flat-handed massage from a cupped one by sound
he describes the masseur's slaps in detail.

games.q: you've practiced calm above the roaring bath. you've learned what you can. what does Seneca do at the end of the letter?
o: stays, to prove he's the calmest man in Rome.
moves out: why torture himself any longer?
games.why: Seneca admits the test was partly a show. Learn quiet inside, he says, and then, if you can, choose a quieter room.

practice: Let the sounds around you come and go like waves, naming each one lightly: car, voice, hum. Then listen inward to the louder noise, the thoughts, and name a few the same way: plan, worry, wish.
Let both kinds pass, and rest in whatever quiet sits underneath.

wordCard.voice: Tranquillitas. Seneca's word for calm: he practices it over a roaring Roman bath, and still, honestly, decides to move to a quieter room. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: calm, the Stoic quiet of mind; Seneca wrote an essay, De Tranquillitate Animi, on it.

carryVoice: Your line: quiet inside. Even Seneca, in the end, chose a quieter room. Rest well.
